extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners referencing MPEP §2106.04)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing the §101 eligibility analysis for claims that may recite judicial exceptions (abstract ideas, laws of nature, natural phenomena), including the Step 2A (Prong One/Two) and Step 2B inquiries, groupings of abstract ideas, and examination practices for multiple exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prong Two — additional elements must transform judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: For a claim reciting a judicial exception to be eligible, the additional elements (if any) in the claim must "transform the nature of the claim" into a patent-eligible application of the judicial exception, Alice Corp., 573 U.S. at 217, either at Prong Two or in Step 2B. If there are no additional elements in the claim, then it cannot be eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a judicial exception is the only thing recited, or the additional elements merely recite another judicial exception, that is insufficient to integrate the judicial exception into a practical application. After making the appropriate rejection, it is a best practice for the examiner to recommend an amendment, if possible, that would resolve eligibility of the claim (see MPEP §2106.07 for formulating such a rejection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling multiple judicial exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim recites multiple judicial exceptions, examiners should apply the same eligibility analysis regardless of the number of exceptions. Unless it is clear that a claim recites distinct exceptions, care should be taken not to parse the claim into multiple exceptions, particularly in claims involving abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If possible, treat the claim as containing a single judicial exception for Prong Two and Step 2B. If multiple exceptions are distinct (e.g., a law of nature and an abstract idea), examiners may select one exception and conduct the eligibility analysis for that one selected exception. If the analysis shows the claim has additional elements that integrate the selected exception into a practical application or amount to significantly more, the claim should be considered eligible. If not, and no other elements amount to significantly more, the claim should be considered ineligible. (See University of Utah Research Foundation v. Ambry Genetics as example.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract idea groupings — identification framework
rubrics_metrics.description: To identify abstract ideas, the Office has enumerated groupings distilled from case law: (1) Mathematical concepts; (2) Certain methods of organizing human activity; (3) Mental processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should identify the specific limitation(s) believed to recite an abstract idea and determine whether the identified limitation(s) fall within at least one of these groupings. The groupings are rooted in Supreme Court and Federal Circuit precedent and are intended to focus examiners on applying the body of case law generally rather than relying on individual cases. See MPEP §2106.04(a)(2) for further discussion of their relationship to precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong One — identification procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether a claim recites an abstract idea by (1) identifying the specific limitation(s) in the claim that the examiner believes recites an abstract idea, and (2) determining whether the identified limitation(s) fall within at least one of the enumerated groupings of abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the identified limitations fall within at least one grouping, the claim is reasonably concluded to recite an abstract idea and requires further analysis in Step 2A Prong Two. If the identified limitations do not fall within any grouping, it is reasonable to find that the claim does not recite an abstract idea and the abstract idea exception inquiry concludes (eligible at Pathway B) unless the claim recites another judicial exception (law of nature or natural phenomenon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Groupings may overlap — identify all applicable groupings
rubrics_metrics.description: The abstract idea groupings are not mutually exclusive; some claim limitations may fall within more than one grouping or sub-grouping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should identify at least one abstract idea grouping, but preferably identify all groupings to the extent possible if a claim limitation is determined to fall within multiple groupings, and then proceed with the Step 2A Prong Two analysis. Example: a formula that could be performed in the human mind may fall within both the mathematical concepts and mental processes groupings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of claims that do not recite abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-limiting hypothetical examples of claims that do not recite (set forth or describe) an abstract idea include: (i) a printer comprising a belt, roller, printhead, ink cartridge; (ii) a washing machine with tub, drive motor, controller; (iii) an earring with a glucose sensor and memory; (iv) a method for sequencing BRCA1 gene sequences by PCR and sequencing; (v) a method for loading BIOS into a local computer system by requesting and transferring BIOS from a remote memory; (vi) a method of rearranging icons on a GUI based on usage determined by processor-tracked memory allocation; (vii) a two-stage neural network training method using transformed facial images and non-facial images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the identified limitations do not fall into any abstract-idea grouping, conclude the claim is eligible at Step 2A Prong One (Pathway B), except in rare circumstances discussed elsewhere (MPEP §2106.04(a)(3)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical concepts grouping (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mathematical concepts grouping is defined as mathematical relationships, mathematical formulas or equations, and mathematical calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court and Federal Circuit have identified various kinds of mathematical concepts as abstract ideas (e.g., Benson, Flook, Diehr, Bilski). When determining whether a claim recites a mathematical concept, examiners should consider whether the claim actually recites the mathematical concept or merely limitations that are based on or involve a mathematical concept. A limitation merely based on or involving a mathematical concept (e.g., using math to implement a particular configuration) may not fall in the grouping if the mathematical concept itself is not recited in the claim. Note that mathematical concepts need not be expressed in symbols — words operating on data can serve the same purpose as formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical relationship is a relationship between variables or numbers; it may be expressed in words or using mathematical symbols (e.g., pressure p = F/A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: a relationship between reaction rate and temperature (Arrhenius equation, Diehr); conversion between binary coded decimal and pure binary (Benson); mathematical relationships between antenna conductor arrangement and radio activity (Mackay Radio); organizing/manipulating information through mathematical correlations (Digitech).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical formulas or equations
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that recites a numerical formula or equation (or a textual replacement for one, e.g., "determining a ratio of A to B") is considered in the mathematical concepts grouping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include electromagnetic standing wave formula (Mackay Radio); the Arrhenius equation (Diehr); a formula for computing an alarm limit (Parker v. Flook); a mathematical formula for hedging (Bilski). Textually-stated calculations like "calculating the force by multiplying mass and acceleration" are treated as formulas (F = ma).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical calculation is a mathematical operation or an act of calculating using mathematical methods to determine a variable or number (e.g., performing exponentiation or other arithmetic operations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim will be considered to fall in this subgroup if, under its broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the specification, it recites such a calculation. Examples include resampled statistical analysis to generate a distribution (SAP America v. InvestPic), calculating alarm limit values (Flook), converting geospatial coordinates to natural numbers (Burnett), managing an insurance policy via calculations (Bancorp), algorithmic optimization of visits (In re Maucorps), and calculating differences between local and average values (In re Abele). A claim does not need to use the word "calculating" to fall here — terms like "determining" or "performing" a mathematical operation may suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certain methods of organizing human activity (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: This grouping covers concepts relating to: (a) fundamental economic principles or practices (including hedging, insurance, mitigating risk); (b) commercial or legal interactions (contracts, legal obligations, advertising/marketing/sales activities, business relations); and (c) managing personal behavior or relationships or interactions between people (including social activities, teaching, following rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all methods of organizing human activity are abstract ideas. The qualifier "certain" limits the grouping to the enumerated sub-groupings and those activities falling within them. The determination should be based on whether the activity itself falls within one of the sub-groupings, not merely on the number of people involved. Activity involving a person and a computer may fall within the grouping when it aligns with the enumerated sub-groupings (e.g., anonymous loan shopping using a mobile phone). Expansion beyond the enumerated sub-groupings should be rare (see MPEP §2106.04(a)(3)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental economic practices or principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Fundamental economic practices/principles encompass concepts relating to the economy and commerce such as hedging, insurance, and mitigating risks; courts have identified practices like hedging and price optimization as fundamental economic concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term "fundamental" does not require being old or well-known — novel economic methods can still be fundamental. Examples and cases: hedging (Bilski), mitigating settlement risk (Alice), rules for wagering games (In re Smith), offer-based price optimization (OIP Technologies), local processing of payments (Inventor Holdings), using markings on mail to communicate sender/recipient/content (Secured Mail Solutions), placing orders based on displayed market information (Trading Technologies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial or legal interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: This sub-group includes agreements in the form of contracts, legal obligations, advertising, marketing or sales activities or behaviors, and business relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: transaction performance guaranties/creating contractual relationships (buySAFE v. Google), managing a stable value protected life insurance policy (Bancorp), processing insurance claims under a policy (Accenture v. Guidewire), tax-free real estate exchanges and aggregation tools (Fort Properties), advertising-as-exchange methods (Ultramercial). Claims directed to creating or implementing contractual/legal/marketing interactions may be directed to an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental processes grouping
rubrics_metrics.description: Mental processes are concepts performed in the human mind, including observation, evaluation, judgment, and opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claim limitations are concepts that a human can perform mentally (even if aided by a computer), they may fall in this grouping. Claims that merely involve mental steps or human thought processes require careful analysis and, if found to recite abstract ideas, proceed to Step 2A Prong Two to determine whether additional elements integrate the idea into a practical application.
